long.title: Why Did Abraham Leave Everything? | The Full Story of Abram's Call | Genesis 12-13 (KJV)
long.first_comment: In Egypt he asked his wife to lie to save himself. On the hill he gave Lot the best land. Which Abram are you more like today?

narration.text: That is not a coward in some story you have never heard. That is Abram, the man the whole Bible calls the father of faith.
Only a few months earlier, God had promised to bless him and to make his name great. Now, at the border of Egypt, he is afraid for his life, and he is asking his wife to lie for him.
How does a man go from hearing the voice of God to this? To understand it, we have to go back to the day he left everything without knowing where he was going.
This is the full story of the call of Abram, Genesis twelve and thirteen, word for word from the King James Bible. And it is far more honest than most of us remember.
Abram lived in Haran, a trading town far to the north. His father had died there. He was seventy-five, and his wife Sarai had never had a child.
Remember where we left the world. At Babel, people tried to make a name for themselves, and God scattered them. Now, out of all those scattered nations, God speaks to one old man with no son.
Now the Lord had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father’s house, unto a land that I will shew thee:
Notice what God does not tell him. He does not name the land. He does not say how far, or how long, or what it will cost. He only says: go, and I will show you.
And I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and make thy name great; and thou shalt be a blessing:
And I will bless them that bless thee, and curse him that curseth thee: and in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed.
Seven promises. And one word to hold on to: all.
In that world your father's house was your name, your land and your protection. To leave it was to become a stranger with no rights.
And God asked him to leave exactly that.
So Abram departed, as the Lord had spoken unto him; and Lot went with him: and Abram was seventy and five years old when he departed out of Haran.

And Abram took Sarai his wife, and Lot his brother’s son, and all their substance that they had gathered, and the souls that they had gotten in Haran; and they went forth to go into the land of Canaan; and into the land of Canaan they came.
Here is an honest question. Would you go, to a place God has only promised to show you?
And Abram passed through the land unto the place of Sichem, unto the plain of Moreh. And the Canaanite was then in the land.

That last sentence matters. The land was not empty. It was full of other people, with their own towns, their own gods and their own claims. Abram arrived as a guest in the land that was promised to him.
And the Lord appeared unto Abram, and said, Unto thy seed will I give this land: and there builded he an altar unto the Lord, who appeared unto him.
Unto thy seed. But Abram had no child at all. So he answered the only way he could: he built an altar, a heap of field stones that said, here God spoke to me, and I believed.

And he removed from thence unto a mountain on the east of Beth–el, and pitched his tent, having Beth–el on the west, and Hai on the east: and there he builded an altar unto the Lord, and called upon the name of the Lord.
Tent and altar. The tent says he is only passing through. The altar says Who he is passing through with.
And Abram journeyed, going on still toward the south.
And then, in the land of promise, the rain stopped.
And there was a famine in the land: and Abram went down into Egypt to sojourn there; for the famine was grievous in the land.
God brought him here. And here, there is no food.
Notice what is missing. No altar. No prayer. No word from God. For the first time since Haran, Abram decides on his own.
Egypt had the great river, and when the rain failed, the hungry went down there to buy grain.
And it came to pass, when he was come near to enter into Egypt, that he said unto Sarai his wife,
And then he said the words you heard at the very beginning. Say you are my sister.
And the strange part is, it was half true. Later Abram explains that Sarai was his father's daughter, but not his mother's. Not quite a lie. A truth used to hide a lie.
Be honest. How many of our own lies are built exactly like that?
And it came to pass, that, when Abram was come into Egypt, the Egyptians beheld the woman that she was very fair.
The princes also of Pharaoh saw her, and commended her before Pharaoh: and the woman was taken into Pharaoh’s house.
Feel that sentence. The woman was taken, and her husband stood outside, alive, exactly as he had planned.
And he entreated Abram well for her sake: and he had sheep, and oxen, and he asses, and menservants, and maidservants, and she asses, and camels.
He walked into Egypt hungry, and now he is getting rich from his own lie. Every animal in his herd was a payment for his wife. It is one of the most uncomfortable verses in the whole book.
So where is God in this? The man meant to bless the nations has carried a lie into a king's house.
And the Lord plagued Pharaoh and his house with great plagues because of Sarai Abram’s wife.
God stepped in, not for Abram's cleverness, but because of Sarai, the one person in this story who never gets a single word.
And Pharaoh called Abram, and said, What is this that thou hast done unto me? why didst thou not tell me that she was thy wife?
Why saidst thou, She is my sister? so I might have taken her to me to wife: now therefore behold thy wife, take her, and go thy way.
Three questions from a king, and every one of them is fair.
The pagan king asks the moral questions. The man of God has no answer.
And Pharaoh commanded his men concerning him: and they sent him away, and his wife, and all that he had.
He failed, and God did not let go of him. Faith here is not a perfect man holding on to God. It is God holding on to an imperfect man.
And Abram went up out of Egypt, he, and his wife, and all that he had, and Lot with him, into the south.
And Abram was very rich in cattle, in silver, and in gold.
And he went on his journeys from the south even to Beth–el, unto the place where his tent had been at the beginning, between Beth–el and Hai;
Unto the place of the altar, which he had made there at the first: and there Abram called on the name of the Lord.
He went down hungry and came back rich, and the first thing he does is go back to the old altar.
Sometimes the way forward after a failure is the last place you were honest with God.
And Lot also, which went with Abram, had flocks, and herds, and tents.
And the land was not able to bear them, that they might dwell together: for their substance was great, so that they could not dwell together.
Here is the irony. Egypt made them rich, and the riches are what now drive them apart. Too many animals and too little grass.
And there was a strife between the herdmen of Abram’s cattle and the herdmen of Lot’s cattle: and the Canaanite and the Perizzite dwelled then in the land.
Read the last line again. The Canaanite and the Perizzite were watching. The family meant to bless the nations was fighting over water in front of them.
And Abram said unto Lot,
Read that slowly. Abram is the elder. He is the head of the family. By every custom of his world he had the right to choose first, and he gives the choice away.
The man who lied in Egypt to save himself now risks the best of everything to keep the peace. That is what has changed in Abram. Not his talent. His trust.

And Lot lifted up his eyes, and beheld all the plain of Jordan, that it was well watered every where, before the Lord destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, even as the garden of the Lord, like the land of Egypt, as thou comest unto Zoar.
Lot looked, and saw Egypt again: green, watered and rich. And the Bible slips in a warning he could not hear.
Then Lot chose him all the plain of Jordan; and Lot journeyed east: and they separated themselves the one from the other.
Abram dwelled in the land of Canaan, and Lot dwelled in the cities of the plain, and pitched his tent toward Sodom.
But the men of Sodom were wicked and sinners before the Lord exceedingly.
Lot chose with his eyes. He pitched his tent toward Sodom. Not inside it yet. Just facing it. That is how most drifting begins.
Two men looked at the same land. One chose what looked like Egypt and called it wisdom. The other let God choose, and waited to be shown.
And Abram is left in the hard hill country with the poorer land. An old man, still without a son, and now without his nephew too. He has given away the best of everything.
And the Lord said unto Abram, after that Lot was separated from him, Lift up now thine eyes, and look from the place where thou art northward, and southward, and eastward, and westward:
Notice when God speaks again. Not in Egypt, and not while Abram was grabbing. Only after he had let go of the best land, and stood alone on the poorer hill.
Lift up now thine eyes. Lot lifted up his eyes to choose for himself. Now God tells Abram to lift up his eyes and see what God has chosen for him. North, south, east and west.
For all the land which thou seest, to thee will I give it, and to thy seed for ever.
And I will make thy seed as the dust of the earth: so that if a man can number the dust of the earth, then shall thy seed also be numbered.
Try to count the dust on one hillside. You cannot. That is what God promised to a man of seventy-five who still had no child.
Faith is not counting what you can already see. It is trusting the One who promised you what you cannot count, even when your hands are still empty.
Arise, walk through the land in the length of it and in the breadth of it; for I will give it unto thee.
Then Abram removed his tent, and came and dwelt in the plain of Mamre, which is in Hebron, and built there an altar unto the Lord.
Tent and altar. The man who went down to Egypt without a prayer ends at his third altar.
He left everything without knowing where. But the real journey was never across a map. It was from fear to trust, and it took a failure in Egypt for it to begin.
In Egypt he grabbed at his own life and lost his honour. On that hill he let go of the best land, and God gave him everything he could see.
What would you have to let go of to follow God? Tell me below. Next: kings at war, Lot taken captive, and Abram goes after him. Subscribe.
